title: CV Writing and Interview Skills
summary: How to write a focused CV and cover letter, and prepare for and perform well in job interviews.

lessons.title: What a CV is for and how to structure it

body.p: A CV (called a resume in some countries) has one job: to get you an interview. An employer may spend under a minute on a first read, so the document must be easy to scan and show quickly that you fit the role. It is a marketing document about what you can do, not a full autobiography.

list: Contact details: name, phone number, a professional email address and your city. Add a LinkedIn link if it is up to date.
Personal profile: two or three lines stating who you are, your strongest relevant skills and the kind of role you want.
Education: most recent first, with degree, institution, dates and relevant modules, projects or results.
Work experience, internships, volunteering and projects: most recent first, with achievement-focused bullets.
Skills: specific tools and languages, for example Excel, Python, laboratory techniques, or French at conversational level.
Referees: a line saying 'References available on request', or named referees if the employer asks. Always ask permission before naming someone.

body.h: Rules that save you from rejection

list: Keep it to one or two pages. Graduates with limited experience usually fit on one or two.
Use a clean, consistent layout with a readable font and clear headings.
Proofread carefully. Spelling errors suggest carelessness.
Use a professional email address, not a nickname.
Save as PDF unless the employer asks for another format, and use a sensible file name such as Chidi_Eze_CV.pdf.

body.p: Conventions differ by country and employer. In some places a photo, date of birth or marital status are expected, and in others they are not used. Check the employer's instructions and local norms, and give only what is requested and relevant.

Before: 'Hard-working graduate seeking a challenging position in a reputable company.' This could describe anyone. After: 'Final-year Accounting student at the University of Ghana with a three-month audit internship and strong Excel skills. Seeking a graduate role in financial reporting.' The second is specific and tells the reader where you fit. The institution here is only an example; use your own details.

body.tip: Ask a friend to look at your CV for 30 seconds and tell you what they remember. That is roughly what an employer will take away.

body.p: Most weak CVs list duties: what the job description said you should do. Strong CVs show achievements: what you did, how, and what changed because of it. Employers want evidence that you create results, and numbers make results believable.

Start with a strong action verb, say what you did, and end with the outcome or scale. Examples of action verbs: organised, analysed, designed, reduced, trained, negotiated, built, tutored. Use past tense for finished roles and keep each bullet to one or two lines.

body.code:
Before: Responsible for helping customers in a shop.
After:  Served around 60 customers per day at a busy Nairobi retail shop, handling cash and mobile payments with no till discrepancies during a six-month contract.

Before: Treasurer of the Engineering Society.
After:  Managed a society budget of GH¢12,000, introduced a monthly expense report and cut printing costs by 15 percent.

Before: Did a final-year project on solar panels.
After:  Designed and tested a small solar charging system for phones, comparing three panel angles and presenting findings to a panel of lecturers.

body.p: The figures above are illustrations. Only use numbers that are true and that you can explain in an interview. If you do not have exact figures, use honest approximations such as 'around' or 'about', or describe scale: 'for a team of eight' or 'across three campuses'. Never invent results.

Students often have more evidence than they think. Group projects, tutoring, running a club, volunteering, helping at a family business, part-time work and leading a church or community activity all show skills such as teamwork, organisation, communication and reliability. Describe what you did and the outcome, in the same way as for paid work.

steps: List three or four experiences relevant to the job.
For each, write what you did, the tool or method you used, and the result.
Add a number if you honestly can: people, money, time saved, grade or percentage.
Cut any bullet you could not explain confidently in an interview.

body.tip: Avoid vague phrases such as 'team player' and 'good communicator' unless a bullet proves them with an example.

lessons.title: Tailoring your CV and writing a cover letter

body.p: Sending the same CV to every employer is the most common mistake. Employers and many recruitment systems look for evidence that you match the specific role. Tailoring does not mean lying. It means choosing and ordering true information so that the most relevant evidence appears first.

steps: Read the job advert slowly and highlight the required skills, qualifications and responsibilities.
Make a list of the key words and phrases the advert repeats, such as 'data analysis', 'customer service' or 'project coordination'.
Match each requirement with a real experience of yours.
Move the best matches to the top of your CV and rewrite your profile around them.
Use the employer's own terms where they truthfully describe what you did, since some employers use software that scans for keywords.

body.p: A cover letter is a short letter, usually under one page, that explains why you want this role at this organisation and why you are a good fit. It should not repeat the CV line by line. Address it to a named person when you can. If the advert gives no name, use the formal greeting the employer's instructions suggest.

list: Opening paragraph: the role you are applying for and one sentence on why you are interested.
Middle paragraphs: two or three strongest matches between the advert and your experience, each with a specific example.
Closing paragraph: your availability, thanks, and a clear statement that you would welcome an interview.

body.p: Weak: 'I am a hard-working student and I think I would be good in your company.' Stronger: 'Your advert asks for someone who can analyse sales data and present findings. In my final-year project I analysed 18 months of sales records for a local business in Excel and presented three recommendations to the owner, which she used to change her stock ordering.' The second gives evidence that matches the advert.

body.tip: Check the application instructions for file type, length, deadline and required documents. Applications that ignore instructions may be rejected before anyone reads them.

lessons.title: Preparing for the interview and the STAR method

body.p: Good interviews are mostly prepared. The interviewer wants to know whether you can do the job, will fit with the team, and genuinely want this role. Prepare so you can answer those three questions with evidence.

list: Research the organisation: what it does, its products or services, recent news, and its values.
Reread the job description and prepare an example for each main requirement.
Prepare a 60 to 90 second answer to 'Tell me about yourself' covering your background, key strengths and why you want this job.
Prepare answers to common questions: strengths, weaknesses, why this role, why this organisation, and where you see yourself in a few years.
Prepare two or three questions to ask the interviewer.
Plan logistics: your route and travel time, documents to bring, and clothes suitable for the workplace.

body.p: Behavioural questions such as 'Tell me about a time you worked under pressure' ask for a real example. STAR keeps your answer organised. Situation: set the scene briefly. Task: say what you were responsible for. Action: describe what you personally did. Result: give the outcome and what you learned.
Question: 'Tell me about a time you solved a problem in a team.'

body.code:
Situation: In my final year, our four-person group project in Civil Engineering fell behind because two members were both waiting for the same survey data.
Task: As group coordinator, I had to get the project back on schedule before the presentation in two weeks.
Action: I split the work into small tasks with dates, asked one member to collect the data using a shared spreadsheet, and held a ten-minute check-in twice a week.
Result: We submitted two days early and received a good grade. I now use short written plans in any group work.

body.p: Notice that the answer says 'I' for the actions, because the interviewer is assessing you, not the group. It is honest and specific. Practise aloud with a friend or record yourself. Aim for answers of about two minutes, then stop.

body.tip: Prepare four or five STAR stories that can be adapted: teamwork, leadership, a mistake you learned from, a deadline, and a time you dealt with a difficult person.

lessons.title: Interview day, online interviews and follow-up

body.p: First impressions form quickly, so arrive prepared and calm. For an in-person interview, aim to arrive 10 to 15 minutes early. Greet people politely, listen carefully, keep eye contact and speak clearly. Take a copy of your CV, a notepad and your ID or documents if requested.

list: Test your device, internet connection, camera and microphone the day before. If data or power supply is unreliable, have a backup such as a phone hotspot or another location.
Choose a quiet place with light on your face and a plain background.
Close other applications and silence notifications.
Look at the camera when you speak, and keep notes out of sight or short.
Log in a few minutes early and have the interviewer's phone number in case of technical trouble.

body.p: Pause before answering a difficult question. If you do not understand, ask the interviewer to repeat or clarify. If you do not know something, say so honestly and explain how you would find out. When asked about a weakness, name a real one that does not undermine the role and explain what you are doing about it. Never criticise former employers, lecturers or classmates.

Ask questions that show interest: what a typical first month looks like, how success in the role is measured, what training is available, or what the next steps in the process are. Avoid asking about holidays or salary as your first question.

If asked about salary expectations, research typical pay for similar roles in your country and city before the interview, and give a reasonable range or ask about the pay band. Pay norms and employment terms vary, so check the contract carefully and seek proper advice on legal questions. Afterwards, send a short thank-you email within a day, mentioning something specific from the conversation. If you are not selected, ask politely for feedback and use it to improve your next application.

body.tip: After each interview, write down the questions you were asked and how you answered. This builds a personal question bank for the next one.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a CV?
options: To list every job, course and activity you have ever done, in as much detail as possible
To get you an interview by showing you fit the role
To replace the interview
To prove your age and nationality

quiz.q: Which profile statement is the strongest for a graduate applying for a marketing assistant post?
options: Hard-working graduate who is a keen team player seeking a challenging and rewarding position in a good company.
I am a good worker who loves people.
Marketing graduate who grew a student society's Instagram from 300 to 1,200 followers. Seeking an entry-level marketing role.
Please give me a chance to prove myself, because I need a job urgently and will work very hard.

quiz.q: You are not sure whether a photo or date of birth belongs on a CV where you are applying. What is the best action?
options: Always include a photo and your date of birth, because every employer expects them on every CV
Never include anything personal
Copy whatever a friend does
Follow the employer's instructions and local conventions, and include only what is requested and relevant

quiz.q: Which bullet is better CV writing?
options: Responsible for the social media accounts of the faculty and for various communication tasks.
Managed the faculty Instagram account, posting three times a week; followers rose from 400 to 900 in a semester.
Good at social media.
Worked on social media, the faculty website and various other tasks for the department.

quiz.q: You have no formal work experience. What is the most sensible approach?
options: Describe relevant projects, volunteering or leadership with actions and results
Leave out the experience section and fill the page with personal details and a list of hobbies
Invent a job to fill the gap
Exaggerate your grades

quiz.q: A job advert repeatedly mentions 'customer service' and 'cash handling'. You did both in a shop job. What should you do?
options: Make the shop job's bullets on those two skills prominent, using truthful wording
Remove the shop job from the CV because it is not graduate level and does not look impressive
Use the same CV you send to every employer
Add skills you do not have

quiz.q: What should a cover letter mainly do?
options: Copy the CV into paragraph form, so the employer can read the same details in a different layout
Complain about the job market
Explain why you want this role and give examples that match the advert
List your hobbies

quiz.q: Why does the STAR method help in an interview?
options: It lets you avoid giving details that might expose weaknesses in the example you choose
It organises a real example into situation, task, action and result
It guarantees a job offer
It is only for technical questions

quiz.q: In a STAR answer about a group project, why should the Action part focus on 'I' rather than 'we'?
options: The interviewer is assessing your own contribution
Group work is not valued by employers, who only want to hear about individual projects
It makes the answer longer
'We' is grammatically wrong

quiz.q: Your interview is online and your home internet is often unreliable. Which preparation is most useful?
options: Do nothing about it, since an internet connection is outside your control and cannot be improved
Ask for the interview to be cancelled
Test the setup beforehand and arrange a backup such as a phone hotspot and the interviewer's contact number
Turn the camera off

quiz.q: You are asked a question you cannot answer. What is the best response?
options: Invent an answer confidently
Say that the question is unfair and politely ask the interviewer to move on to another topic
Stay silent until the interviewer moves on
Admit it, then explain how you would find the answer

quiz.q: The interviewer asks 'Do you have any questions for us?' Which is the best response?
options: No, I have no questions, because everything was explained clearly during the interview.
How many days of holiday will I get each year if I join?
What is the minimum I need to do?
What does success look like in this role, and what are the next steps?
